answer: Official Go 1.23 release notes and the Go blog establish that a for-range loop can range over iterator functions of the types func(yield func(V) bool) and func(yield func(K, V) bool); the iter package names these iter.Seq[V] and iter.Seq2[K, V]. The iterator is called with a yield function: Seq calls yield(v) for each value, Seq2 calls yield(k, v) for each pair, and both stop early if yield returns false. Secondary analyses describe the compiler translation: the loop body becomes the yield function passed to the iterator, and a break or return in the body makes yield return false so the iterator can stop. A correct iterator must check that return value; continuing to call yield after it returns false panics with 'range function continued iteration after function for loop body returned false'. The iter package also provides Pull and Pull2 to convert push-style iterators into pull-style next and stop functions, and Go 1.23 adds iterator-aware functions in the slices and maps packages. Performance equivalence to hand-written loops is claimed by a secondary article but is not established by the official docs retrieved. The feature was experimental in Go 1.22 behind GOEXPERIMENT=rangefunc according to a secondary blog.
gaps: The official Go 1.23 release notes excerpt retrieved truncates the exact list of accepted iterator function types; the iter package docs and Go blog identify Seq and Seq2, but whether additional accepted signatures exist is not established by the retrieved text. This does not block the supported conclusion that these two signatures are accepted, but it blocks a claim that this is the complete list.

The exact compiler desugaring for labeled break, continue, goto and non-local return in range-over-func loops is described in a secondary compiler analysis (mcyoung) and is not verified against the official language spec in this run. This qualifies detailed compiler-mechanics conclusions but not the basic break/return behavior supported by the retrieved sources.
Performance equivalence to hand-written loops rests on one secondary article; no benchmark or official performance claim was retrieved, so it cannot be concluded as established.

The Go 1.22 GOEXPERIMENT=rangefunc detail comes from a secondary blog, not official Go 1.22 documentation, so the experimental-availability claim is attributed rather than verified against a primary record.

The retrieved 2022 design discussion states that the yield function will panic if called after the loop is done or from the wrong goroutine, but this run did not verify whether the final Go 1.23 documentation states the same rule for wrong-goroutine calls.

interpretation: The question asks how Go 1.23 range-over-func iterators work. I read this primarily as asking for the language semantics and usage: what types can be ranged over, how the loop body and iterator interact, how early termination works, and what the standard library adds. A second reading is compiler implementation: how the compiler desugars the loop and handles break, continue, goto and return. A third reading is practical/performance: how to write custom iterators and whether they perform like hand-written loops. The answer covers the semantic reading directly, notes the compiler-desugaring account from secondary analyses, and treats performance equivalence as a secondary claim rather than an established official fact.

claims.claim: In Go 1.23, the range clause in a for-range loop accepts iterator functions of certain types as range expressions.
claims.note: The Go 1.23 release notes state that the range clause now accepts iterator functions as range expressions, which is the claim.

claims.claim: The accepted iterator function types include func(yield func(V) bool) and func(yield func(K, V) bool).
claims.note: The range-functions blog says Seq and Seq2 are the iterator function types usable with for/range and defines them with exactly the two signatures named in the claim.

claims.claim: The iter package defines Seq[V any] as func(yield func(V) bool).
claims.note: The blog's iter package definition gives Seq exactly as func(yield func(V) bool).

claims.claim: The iter package defines Seq2[K, V any] as func(yield func(K, V) bool).
claims.note: The blog's iter package definition gives Seq2 exactly as func(yield func(K, V) bool).

claims.claim: When a Seq is called as seq(yield), it calls yield(v) for each value v in the sequence.
claims.note: The iter package documentation for Seq states that seq(yield) calls yield(v) for each value in the sequence.

claims.claim: When a Seq2 is called as seq(yield), it calls yield(k, v) for each pair (k, v) in the sequence.
claims.note: The iter package documentation defines Seq2 together with Seq as shorthands for iterators that pass 1 or 2 values per sequence element to yield; Seq2 is the two-value case, i.e. yield(k, v) per pair. (The Seq2-specific type paragraph is truncated in the supplied excerpt, but the general definition explicitly names Seq2.)

claims.claim: A Seq stops early if yield returns false.
claims.note: The Seq documentation states that iteration stops early if yield returns false.

claims.claim: A Seq2 stops early if yield returns false.
claims.note: The iter package defines iterators (Seq and Seq2 among them) as stopping when yield returns false; Seq2 is one of those defined iterators, so it stops early on a false return.

claims.claim: The Go compiler translates a range-over-function loop into calls of the iterator function, passing the loop body as the yield function.
claims.note: Eli Bendersky says the compiler substitutes the yield function for the body of the original range loop, and the DoltHub article says the compiler converts the range loop into function calls; together these establish the claimed desugaring.

claims.claim: A break or return in the loop body causes the yield function to return false, signaling the iterator to stop early.
claims.note: The supplied material establishes only the break half: Eli Bendersky states that a break in the body is transformed into return false from the yield function. The material given does not state that a return in the loop body likewise makes yield return false, so the 'or return' part is not covered.

claims.claim: If an iterator continues calling yield after yield has returned false, the program panics with the runtime error 'range function continued iteration after function for loop body returned false'.
claims.note: The DoltHub article's broken-iterator example shows the exact runtime panic message quoted in the claim.

claims.claim: iter.Pull converts a push-style iterator sequence (Seq) into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop functions.
claims.note: The iter package documentation for Pull states it converts a push-style sequence into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop.

claims.claim: iter.Pull2 converts a push-style Seq2 into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop functions.
claims.note: The iter package documentation for Pull2 states it converts the push-style iterator sequence into a pull-style iterator accessed by next and stop; Pull2 is the Seq2 variant of the function.

claims.claim: Go 1.23 adds functions in the slices package that work with iterators.
claims.note: The range-functions blog states that new in Go 1.23 are functions in the slices package that work with iterators.

claims.claim: Go 1.23 adds functions in the maps package that work with iterators.
claims.note: The same Go 1.23 blog statement covers the maps package functions that work with iterators; the release notes likewise list maps additions.

claims.claim: Before Go 1.23, range-over-function could be tried in Go 1.22 by setting GOEXPERIMENT=rangefunc.
claims.note: The Ardan Labs article states that to try range-over functions in Go 1.22 one must set GOEXPERIMENT to rangefunc, matching the claim.

claims.claim: A motivation for the range-over-function feature was that Go had no standard way to iterate over a sequence of values.
claims.note: The 2022 design discussion (rsc) opens with the statement that Go had no standard way to iterate over a sequence of values, which is the motivation the claim attributes to it.

claims.claim: A secondary article states that range-over-function loops can perform as well as hand-written loops because the Go compiler can inline and optimize them, reducing overhead especially for simple cases.
claims.note: The claim is only that a secondary article states this performance claim; the Medium article states it in essentially the claimed terms, including inlining/optimizing and reduced overhead for simple cases.

conclusions.statement: In Go 1.23, a for-range loop can range over an iterator function of type func(yield func(V) bool) or func(yield func(K, V) bool); the compiler passes the loop body as the yield function, and the iterator calls yield for each element.
Iteration stops early when yield returns false, which is how break and return in the loop body terminate a range-over-func loop.
conclusions.blocked: c10 partial: The supplied material establishes only the break half: Eli Bendersky states that a break in the body is transformed into return false from the yield function. The material given does not state that a return in the loop body likewise makes yield return false, so the 'or return' part is not covered.

conclusions.statement: A correct iterator must stop when yield returns false; if it continues calling yield after a false return, the program panics with 'range function continued iteration after function for loop body returned false'.
The iter package standardizes the iterator types as iter.Seq and iter.Seq2 and provides iter.Pull and iter.Pull2 to convert push-style sequences into pull-style next and stop functions.
Go 1.23 adds iterator-aware functions in the slices and maps packages.

The feature was motivated by the absence of a standard way to iterate over a sequence of values in Go, and it was available experimentally in Go 1.22 behind GOEXPERIMENT=rangefunc before the Go 1.23 release.
A secondary article claims performance equivalence between range-over-function loops and hand-written loops, but the official documentation retrieved does not establish that performance equivalence.
conclusions.blocked: it does not follow from its claims: c18 only establishes that a secondary article makes the performance claim; the conclusion's second conjunct ('the official documentation retrieved does not establish that performance equivalence') is a claim about the official documentation that c18 says nothing about. A premise about what the official docs do or do not establish is missing, so the conclusion does not follow from its listed premise.

conclusions.statement: A Seq stops early if yield returns false, and a Seq2 stops early if yield returns false.

A secondary article states that range-over-function loops can perform as well as hand-written loops because the Go compiler can inline and optimize them, reducing overhead especially for simple cases.
